prompt.context: Our client, High Peaks Jacket Company is a manufacturer of ski apparel located in Vermont. The company currently sells its products through specialty outdoors stores and ski shops throughout the U.S. After two years of flat revenue and profits the company has asked us to identify new avenues for growth.
prompt.question: What should High Peaks do to jumpstart growth?

clarifying_info.q: What are the company's current financials?
clarifying_info.a: High Peaks has $20M in sales and net income of $2M.

clarifying_info.q: What does 'Other' represent in the product exhibit?
clarifying_info.a: 'Other' represents various players with less than 5% market share.

exhibits.title: Channels Exhibit
exhibits.shows: Revenue split by distribution channel (specialty stores, chain stores, internet) for the industry, including each channel's growth rate
exhibits.data: Distribution channels with revenue share and growth rates by channel

exhibits.title: Product Exhibit
exhibits.shows: Revenue by product category (Fleece, Jackets, Pants) segmented by leading manufacturers including High Peaks, North Face, Patagonia, Mountain Hardware, Marmot, Spyder, Cloudveil, and Other
exhibits.data: Market share by product and manufacturer; High Peaks currently does not compete in Pants

exhibits.title: Pricing Data
exhibits.shows: Pricing structure table showing retail price, retailer margin, High Peaks revenue, manufacturing cost, shipping cost, and contribution margin at current pricing and under a 10% price cut scenario, plus volume and profit impact
exhibits.data: Current: Retail $200, Retailer margin 50% ($100), HP Revenue $100, Mfg Cost $50, Shipping $10, Contribution Margin $40; Price Cut: Retail $180, HP Revenue $90, Contribution Margin $30; Volume: 100 -> 120 units (+20%); Revenue: $20,000 -> $21,600; Profits: $4,000 -> $3,600

framework: Use the 4 P's framework: Price, Product, Place (channels/geographies), Promotion
Place – New Channels: evaluate distribution channel mix and growth rates
Place – New Geographies: assess international expansion opportunities
Product – New Products: assess product line gaps vs. competitors
Price – Pricing Adjustments: evaluate elasticity and margin impact of price changes

questions.prompt: Walk through observations from the Channels Exhibit and recommend which channels High Peaks should expand into.
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: (1) Chain stores represent the majority of industry sales with the 2nd highest growth rate; (2) Specialty stores are the slowest growing channel; (3) Internet is the smallest channel but the fastest growing. Candidate should recommend expanding into Internet and chain stores. Exceptional answer notes: Internet is likely highest-margin; chain stores carry risks of margin pressure and brand dilution/channel conflict with specialty retailers; therefore prioritize Internet first and conduct further research on chain stores before committing.

questions.prompt: Walk through observations from the Product Exhibit and recommend which product categories High Peaks should prioritize.
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: (1) Fleece is the largest market but highly concentrated — North Face, Patagonia, and Mountain Hardware hold large shares and High Peaks has a weak relative position; (2) Jackets is less concentrated and High Peaks has solid market share, roughly in line with Patagonia and Marmot; (3) Pants is the least concentrated market with over 50% held by 'Other' and no single player above 20% — High Peaks does not currently compete here. Candidate should recommend expanding into Pants (attractive structure + manufacturing synergies with Jackets) and potentially reducing focus on Fleece. Exceptional answer suggests considering acquiring Spyder or Cloudveil to gain entry into Pants while strengthening existing market positions.

questions.prompt: If the company cuts prices by 10% they believe they can increase sales by 20%. Is this a good idea?
questions.guidance: The answer is No. The price cut reduces per-unit contribution margin and the volume increase is insufficient to offset it, resulting in a net decline in profits from $4,000 to $3,600. Candidate must walk through the math systematically using the pricing data.

math.setup: Compare total profits under current pricing vs. 10% price cut scenario. Use per-unit economics and then scale by volume.
steps: Current: HP Revenue = $100/unit, Mfg Cost = $50, Shipping = $10, Contribution Margin = $40/unit
Price Cut (-10%): Retail $200 -> $180, retailer keeps 50% margin, so HP Revenue = $90/unit
Price Cut profits at 120 units: $30 x 120 = $3,600
Revenue check: Current $100 x 100 = $10,000 (per exhibit uses 200 units base: $20,000); Price Cut $90 x 120 = $10,800 (per exhibit: $21,600) — revenue increases but profits fall
math.answer: No. Despite a 20% volume increase, profits decline from $4,000 to $3,600 (-10%) because the per-unit contribution margin drops from $40 to $30, a 25% reduction that exceeds the 20% volume gain.

questions.prompt: If the company were to expand geographically beyond its US base, what other markets should it explore? Where should it expand first?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify markets where skiing is popular and/or climates are cold: Canada, the Alps (Europe), Scandinavia, the Andes. Canada is the best first choice: closest geographic proximity, similar market characteristics to the US, shared language, and decent market size.

questions.prompt: How large is the Canadian market for ski jackets? (Market sizing)
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a bottoms-up estimate segmenting skiers and non-skiers who buy ski jackets, then adjust for purchase frequency and average price.

math.setup: Segment Canadian population into skiers and non-skiers; estimate annual jacket purchases using jacket lifespan; multiply by average price.
steps: Skier participation rate: 20% => Total skiers: 30M x 20% = 6M
Non-skiers likely to buy a ski jacket: 1/4 => Non-skier jacket buyers: 24M x 0.25 = 6M
Jacket lifespan: 5 years => annual purchase rate: 1/5 = 0.2 jackets/year
math.answer: The Canadian ski jacket market is approximately $360M per year.

brainstorming.prompt: What are possible new avenues for growth for High Peaks across the 4 P's?

categories.name: Place – New Channels
ideas: Enter chain sporting goods stores (e.g., REI, Dick's Sporting Goods)

categories.name: Place – New Geographies
ideas: Japan and South Korea ski markets

categories.name: Product – New Products
ideas: Enter ski pants category (synergies with jacket manufacturing)
Develop fleece accessories (gloves, hats, base layers)
Develop technical softshell or hardshell products
Consider acquisition of Spyder or Cloudveil

categories.name: Price – Pricing Strategy
ideas: Test premium pricing to reinforce brand positioning
Explore tiered pricing across product lines
Use promotional pricing selectively for new channel entry

recommendation: High Peaks should pursue growth primarily through new distribution channels and product expansion rather than price cuts
In the near term, launch an internet direct-to-consumer channel as the fastest-growing, likely highest-margin channel with lowest execution risk
Expand into the ski pants category to capture an underserved, fragmented market where High Peaks can leverage existing manufacturing capabilities and retailer relationships
risks: Entering chain stores risks brand dilution and channel conflict with the specialty store base
Pants line entry requires upfront R&D and manufacturing investment
International expansion introduces FX, logistics, and local regulatory complexity
next_steps: Conduct detailed margin analysis of internet vs. chain store channel economics
Develop pants product line leveraging existing design/manufacturing infrastructure
Commission consumer research on brand perception to assess premium positioning sustainability
Evaluate acquisition targets (Spyder, Cloudveil) for accelerated pants market entry
